utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, would you have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume our work, which we haven't been able to work with for quite a while for various reasons. First of all, I want to be sure the interpreters can hear me. I can't see them as clearly as I could in the other courtroom, but I do recognise their voices. The Office of the Prosecutor, can you hear the Judges, representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Nice. Turning to the Defence, can you hear me, represented by Mr. Greaves and Mr. Londrovic? Can the accused hear me as well? We can now resume, and I would like first to welcome back amongst us Judge Riad. We will start with a motion that was filed on Friday, a Defence motion. Perhaps Mr. Greaves could give us some further information about it, and then we will hear whatever comments the Prosecutor wishes to make. I believe that you want this trial to be postponed. Is that correct? Could you explain what you mean? You know this trial has already been interrupted several times. Therefore, we would ask that you explain why you're making this request. I'm sure your reasons are well founded, but after that the Prosecution will respond and the Judges will take their decisions, as it should be. Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course, and I'm most grateful to Your Honour for introducing the matter in a concise way. Thank you very much for that. Your Honour, the position is this, that Your Honour has correctly identified the purpose of the motion as one to adjourn the trial. Can I say straightaway that it is not an application that we make lightly at all for the obvious reasons that Your Honour has mentioned and also because of the obvious point about witnesses who may be inconvenienced if the motion succeeds, and we have only filed this motion after giving it some considerable and careful thought. The position is this: If I just explain a little bit about the background, Your Honours will forgive me for taking a little time. One of the items upon which the Prosecution has indicated that it relies to prove the crime of genocide against Goran Jelisic is a principal list of some 100 people who it is alleged were identified as being in a mass grave found in the Brcko district sometime in 1992, and also upon a second list of SDA or political persons, second list of some 39 names. The Defence infer from the existence of the list that the Prosecution's case in respect of them is that those people are exclusively Muslim by ethnic or religious background and that those 100 or 139 people were the victims of a deliberate killing as part of a concerted plan to destroy, in whole or in part, the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Defence do not accept necessarily that those people are either all dead or that they were killed as part of such a plan, and as part of its case, the Defence intends to ask of witnesses from the Brcko area about the names of people on those lists and what they know, if anything, of the circumstances of their death or, indeed, whether they know that they are still alive. At least one witness who is due to give evidence, and I won't mention his name, speaks of some of those named on the list in his witness statement, gives them by name, and describes them, for example, as having been killed during an evacuation. It may well be that from such a witness or from witnesses information may be forthcoming which demonstrates that far from having been killed as part of a deliberate policy of liquidating Muslims, the persons named on the lists, or some of them, were in fact killed during ordinary military operations, for example, by shelling directed by one party against the fixed positions of another, or during some localised skirmish between two opposing groups of infantry, or, indeed, that they may have died from causes unconnected with the strife in Brcko. Very recented, as recently as the 17th of August of this year, an investigator employed by the Defence, who is an advocate based in Belgrade in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, became aware of the existence -- or having become aware of the existence of a court at a place called Maoca, which is in the Federation area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is a court which has been set up as an institution to deal with legal matters that would otherwise be within the jurisdiction of the District Court at Brcko. It has been set up, as I understand it, for those people who live in the Federation who are afraid to travel to Brcko but who wish to deal with matters that would ordinarily come within the Brcko Court jurisdiction, in other words, people who used to live in Brcko, their affairs were in Brcko, but they are no longer sufficiently happy to go to Brcko to deal with those affairs, so a secondary court has been set up, as it were, in parallel. He went to that court on the 17th of August and, during the course of making enquires there, became aware that that court held quite large numbers of files which are applications by people to have members of their family declared dead. That, I suspect, is the kind of application which exists in every jurisdiction. I'm sure in each of Your Honours' jurisdictions there are applications where people have gone missing, to have them formally declared dead so that finality can be brought to the affairs of the person who has gone missing. Prior to discovering this fact, the Defence had believed that only the Court at Brcko had jurisdiction over such matters and that only the Court at Brcko had been dealing with such matters. If I might just briefly describe what one might expect to accompany such applications, it is likely that each application will be supported, amongst other things, by affidavit evidence from members of the family and other persons who were aware of the circumstances of the death of the subject of the proceedings. From our own experience of other people, we have traced family members in respect of files held at Brcko of a similar nature. We believe that such information will reveal quite detailed information about the circumstances of the death of the people who are subject of the application, and in some of the cases that we've found, and we anticipate putting before the Court in due course, some of those reveal, far from being killed as part of a deliberate policy, they were in fact killed during the course, as I have described it, of military operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. You are already making your defence arguments. I would like to know what the purpose of the request for the adjournment of this trial is. Let's get back to the purpose, or otherwise this is part of arguing or pleadings that you will have the opportunity to do. What we are interested in right now, we, the Judges, is what your argument is, and that can be defended from your point of view, but we want to know whether that justifies adjournment of this trial. That's the real question at issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I hope that Your Honour will bear with me. I had just been explaining exactly the kernel of what the importance of these documents is, and if Your Honour will forgive me, I would like to make quite clear why they're important to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But please be concise, be precise, because for the time being, I take the liberty of telling to you that we are starting with considerations which are legitimate from the point of view of the defence of your client, but which for the time being do not explain why this trial should be adjourned. Therefore try to be concise and to move forward. I give you back the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The investigator sought to get photocopies of the files. To cut a long story short, he was prevented from so doing and was invited to address himself to the Ministry of Justice. He has written to the Ministry of Justice; they have replied, declining to give him the documents and referring him back, effectively, to the Court at Maoca to obtain these documents. We do not yet have the documents. The Defence are not, at the present time, therefore, in possession of some 59 files which deal with a part of the Prosecution's case, we say a major part of the Prosecution's case. The files may well contain evidence which contradicts that of Prosecution witnesses. They may contain evidence which demonstrates that people died otherwise than in the course of a deliberate policy of liquidation, of genocide. They may also lead to other people being found who can throw light on the death of others named on the list, and it may also contain information which undermines any assertion that a mass grave found in 1992 can be related to these incidents. So these are matters which go to the absolute heart of the Prosecution's case, to wit, to genocide. We say that that is important evidence which ought to be in the possession of the Defence prior to it cross-examining Prosecution witnesses. Without full knowledge of what is in those files, it makes it, we say, very difficult to properly cross-examine Prosecution witnesses at this stage, particularly if, for example, information is contained in a file which reveals that somebody does know, one of the Prosecution witnesses does know something about it, or if it contradicts that which is said by the Prosecution witness. As I say, we don't make the application lightly, but we respectfully submit that this information, going as it does to the heart of a major part of the Prosecution's case, we are entitled to ask witnesses what they know about those people, and we are entitled to ask those witnesses about that with full knowledge, and we submit that those files are absolutely fundamental to enable the Defence to properly cross-examine Prosecution witnesses, and that justice cannot be done unless we are in a position to do that. I have no doubt complaint will be made: "Well, this comes all very late in the day." Could I remind Your Honour that for some two and a half months of this year, investigators who live in Belgrade have not exactly been able freely to travel in the Federation area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that has made a considerable difference to the efficiency with which we have been able to discharge our duties of investigating these matters, and that in part explains why it's only lately that our investigator has been able to travel freely and go to this court in Maoca. That's one of the problems that has faced us, as I suspect it's faced other Defence teams in other trials in this unfortunate summer that we've had. Your Honour, that's the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Greaves. Although the essential purpose of this motion is an adjournment because in light of what is going on in the region, in respect of the files of those who are now missing, the Defence would need those files so that its own investigators could use them in order to cross-examine the witnesses that Mr. Nice wants to call. There, Mr. Nice, is the Defence motion. Perhaps a question before we give the floor to

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does your investigator think that he will be able to have access to those files in a certain amount of time? How long does he need in order to have access to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The problem is, I'm afraid, this, and I didn't tell Your Honour the whole story because you asked me to be brief, but I'll tell you. He initially thought he was going to be given the documents, and whilst he was in the process of obtaining them from one of the judges who has conduct of the matters at that court, another judge came along and said, "It's stopped. Don't do that. Check with the president of the court." The president of the court, when he was spoken to, said, "You must address yourselves to the Ministry of Justice." Having addressed ourselves to the Ministry of Justice, the Ministry of Justice said, "No, nothing to do with us. You must go back to the court." So we're now in a position where we have to go back to the court. It's possible that a refusal will take place, and that would force us to come back to Your Honour and ask Your Honour to issue a request to Bosnia-Herzegovina to yield up the documents. But I'm looking a little bit further ahead. Of course, they are in Bosnia, I suspect, and they would need still to be translated if they are to be of any use to me. That's another problem that faces us. But yes, Your Honour has identified the purpose to which they would be put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would be entirely inappropriate for an adjournment to be granted, in our respectful submission. The fruit of inquiries at this particular Court is probably no different from the fruit of inquiry at the Brcko court itself. I don't know if my friends have access to all the Brcko court inquiries, and it doesn't matter if they do or not, because there may yet be further applications before that court in respect of people not yet the subject of application, in the same way as there may be yet further applications in respect of other names and at the other court yet to come. So in principle, the fruit of these other courts is unlikely to be helpful or critical or central to any aspect of this case, and it is wholly uncertain when, in any event, any such material should be forthcoming. But that is but a minor point of argument compared with the substantial reasons why this application, coming as late as it does, should be rejected. First, what is the Prosecution's case in relation to the list? Is it the absolutely central piece of evidence that the Defence categorise it so to be? No. The central evidence here is the evidence from the eyewitnesses, who reveal quite clearly a campaign of killing, a campaign the nature of which will be properly decided upon from all the live evidence before you, both as to its scale, as to its purpose, as to its targets. And that evidence also, of course, contains plentiful evidence of the state of mind of the defendant Jelisic, one of probably the two important elements upon which this case will focus in due course. That is the central evidence. To that evidence, it's true that there is a list; I'll just tell you a little bit about the list. The list of some 200-plus bodies, of which 100 or so were identified, was a list prepared by officials in the republic in October 1992, and handed over, eventually, via another source, to investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, some years later. The list purports to be a list of people who died and who were buried in unmarked graves, starting in May of 1992. Insofar as there are 100-plus names identified on that list, some eight of them can, in any event, be connected directly to the defendant Jelisic, because he's pleaded guilty in respect of murders of the named people, or eight of the named people, on that list. There are several more names to whom he can be linked by the evidence of witnesses who will say, "There was a killing, Jelisic did or was complicit in the killing, and this is the name of the person." Beyond that, there is evidence of inference in respect of many more names. The names on the list are names of people who were killed at this time. So the list is not a central piece of evidence; it's a piece of evidence that is contemporaneous, in that the list itself emerges from about the time and at the hands of others. It's evidence, insofar as it confirms particular deaths, that corroborates what the Chamber will have heard from elsewhere, and it may be that it will be evidence which will go to show that the scale of the killings was as boasted of by Jelisic and as revealed uncontrovertibly, the Chamber may decide, in the evidence of the mass graves said in this contemporaneous document to have been filled in 1992 and capable of being shown by other evidence to have been constructed and filled, at least as to one of the graves, in 1992. That piece of evidence, to remind the Chamber, comes in the form of a sequence of photographs, the first sequence being photographs that the defendant has admitted are of his executing a victim outside Brcko police station, the same reel of film ending with a photograph of a mass grave, which was identified by those exhuming the mass grave as being clearly the same grave; they can tell it by the position of the bodies and the bones when exhumed, comparing it with the photograph of the grave at the time. So that material goes to show the contemporaneity with Jelisic's killings of the mass graves. This is all material quite independent of the list. The list confirms some things in parts and may flesh out the picture. It goes no further than that. Now, as to the particular concerns of my learned friend Mr. Greaves, the witnesses, he says, are to be asked about the names on the list. Indeed, for today's witness, I have done that in preparation myself. I've made the list available to him, so that rather than read 100-plus names in a hurry before you, he can look at in detail, reflect, and let you know what, if anything, he knows about the names. And you'll discover that he knows one or two names. Indeed, he also knows the one name that is not a Muslim; there is one Croat who was killed and who he is able to speak of. But he is able to speak of a few names. He is able to say whether any of the people on the list are, to his knowledge, still alive or not. How much further would the Defence be able to go if they had some material going to show that one or other of these people was alive? Probably no further. And if, in the event it ever proves to be desirable for a witness who has been asked about these things to be recalled, they can be recalled. We will always cooperate, and the Chamber has the power to seek the recall, has the power to eliminate from its mind the totality of the evidence, if it so decided, of a witness who, for some reason, declined to be recalled, and thus to safeguard the Defence. But those problems won't arise, because this case is in principal to be decided on the evidence of the witnesses. It may be assisted to a degree by the list. The list can form part, if it's the subject of further evidence, can form part of the Defence case, but it would be wholly wrong for any adjournment to be allowed at this stage. Can I respectfully remind you of the unhappy history of the position of witnesses in this case. On the earlier hearing, some three of the eight witnesses who are now here, waiting to give evidence today, were called to The Hague but not reached. They are here for a second time already. One of the witnesses here today, and I'm not going to identify from which country he has come, but he's travelled a long way to be here. They have all been or are in the process of being prepared to give evidence in a succinct way to this Tribunal. They are therefore already through or part-way through the process both of reviving their memories for the purpose of helping this Tribunal and reliving their experiences, for that is what is required of them, and it would be quite wrong for their evidence not to be taken, in our respectful submission, now. The Chamber will recall that it was difficult to find this tour, as we believe it to be three weeks of sittings starting today, and that we don't know when any further sittings might be available for the taking of this case. I return, therefore, to the way the matter is put. It's put that matters can't be put to these witnesses because the Defence enquires aren't complete. It is unlikely in the extreme that where these witnesses speak of particular individuals who they saw killed, it's unlikely in the extreme that there's going to be a true countercase that the witness is lying about it. The Court will remember, I think, the evidence of the first two witnesses, A and B, and indeed the very limited cross-examination of them which didn't go to the substance of the killings, which are of course admitted by Jelisic, but went to the accompanying words. It is in reality, I think, inconceivable that we are going to find a challenge to the evidence of a direct killing. If there is evidence from a court elsewhere that some name on this list, if the list becomes of value to you, may have died in other circumstances, then either that name will be of no value or maybe the list itself will be devalued, but that doesn't attack the heart of this case at all. These witnesses who have come here in the circumstances I've described should now, in our respectful submission, be heard starting this afternoon. I'll just check with Mr. Tochilovsky to see if there is anything he wishes to add. Thank you, unless I can help you further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The first point that my learned friend raised as to the existence of these files at the Brcko court, I think he must have misunderstood what I said. We've already looked at the Brcko court. Those files which have been found at the other court do not exist at Brcko. So this is the first time we've done that enquiry. It did not reveal any files in relation to these people. It was only at the court at Maoca that revealed the existence of these files. The second matter is this, is that whilst seeking to diminish the importance of the list in his case, my learned friend has, we submit, set out a case as to why the list is, in fact, important. It effectively, he says, supports and fills in, as it were, pieces of the jigsaw, supports the evidence of other witnesses. So in effect what he's saying is it's not just the eyewitness, it is supported by the list. That's why it's important to the Prosecution. They wouldn't be placing it in front of you unless it had that importance. The third matter is this: My learned friend makes a speech in anticipation of the honesty and accuracy of his witnesses. That, of course, is actually a matter for Your Honours. We don't know. Some witness may come along who has an intention not to be truthful or accurate, and if one of those files was to reveal that a witness wasn't being truthful or accurate, then that would be of extreme importance. He, of course, is supremely confident, as prosecutors always are, that their witnesses are honest, truthful, and accurate, but regrettably he may not be right about that. The position is that there may be information in these files which demonstrates that the witness is untruthful or perhaps more likely is inaccurate. Because of the passage of time and events of this kind, a name may be misunderstood or misheard and information come out that is inaccurate and which misleads Your Honour. That would be wrong, if Your Honour were to be given information which was, in fact, incorrect. We submit that the possession of these files may assist the Prosecution, but the Defence say that in the interests of the truth-finding process, these files are of supreme importance and it would be very difficult, we submit, properly and effectively and, we say, with confidence to cross-examine the witnesses. I hear what my learned friend says about the witnesses having been here before. It is partly for that reason that I say we make this application -- we do not make this application lightly, and we have considered that issue before making this motion before Your Honours. But we do it and we place it before you and invite Your Honours to accede to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the Judges deliberate, let me ask you whether you have considered, Mr. Greaves, according to Rule 73 ter, that once all its evidence is completed by the Prosecution during a Pre-trial Conference, all of the defence will be reviewed, and perhaps at that point this type of question could arise, a question which the Judges could then decide. Have you clearly looked at this text, this Rule of our proceedings? Secondly, did you also measure the fact that today, in the three weeks of trial days after which -- Mr. Fourmy can't be here today, but after that there is going to be a break in the trial which perhaps you could use in order to obtain what you need for the presentation of your Defence evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As to the first matter, Your Honour, I had not considered Rule 73 ter, I must confess. Your Honour, I think the way in which we have put our case rather suggests that we consider it important that it should be done during the course of the Prosecution's evidence. Of course, by the time Rule 73 ter comes into operation, the Prosecution's case will have closed and be finished, and I don't see how we could then rectify that which had taken place. As far as the second matter that Your Honour related that dealt with this concern, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me interrupt you for a moment, please. Excuse me. By calling back the witness or witnesses to whom you would like to ask further questions once you have the files, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that would be part of a re-opened Prosecution case. We would not want to be responsible for calling witnesses who are hostile to our case. That would be very unfair. The second matter Your Honour raised, the question of the period after the end of this sitting, of course we shall be making efforts to get hold of these files in the meantime, but, as we say, by that time the witnesses will have come and gone. Some may be reluctant to return for whatever reason -- who knows -- if asked to be recalled. It's difficult for inferences to be drawn, one way or the other, if no reason is given or someone simply says, "I'm not prepared to travel yet again." It's very difficult to go and say that, and the Defence would then be in the position where we have this information and the witness has not been able to be asked about it or to deal with it. That leaves the state of evidence in a very unsatisfactory state, we would submit, unsatisfactory because, as it were, all the loose ends have not been tied up. Your Honours will be left in a situation where a question mark is raised but is unresolved over a witness's evidence. Quite plainly, as far as this witness who is due to give evidence this afternoon is concerned, he plainly knows something of some people on the list. That demonstrates clearly that we're likely to have more of it. That, we would submit, if any question mark were to be left, would be most unsatisfactory and unjust. Is there anything else upon which I can assist either Your Honour or Your Honour's colleagues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me turn to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges are going to deliberate, and we will resume the hearing at quarter after 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume the hearing. Please be seated. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before Your Honour announces the decision, may I just add something? I explained to your associate that I needed to add something. One of the problems of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the debate is closed now. I don't think there is anything further to say. Now the Judges are going to render their decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand that, and, of course, if the decision is there should be no adjournment, there's no problem. The difficulty was that, with a motion that comes late on a Friday afternoon, undetected errors can slip through, and I discovered something favourable to my position and unfavourable to the Defence application only after you arose, and from looking at the list that Mr. Greaves is working on, and I desire to correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I don't want to reopen this discussion, Mr. Nice. That isn't appropriate, because if we reopen the discussion, we've got to give the floor back to Mr. Greaves. I believe the Judges have heard your arguments, and they will now render their decision. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Nice. Thank you for your comprehension. The Judges, hearing or reviewing the Defence brief on Goran Jelisic of the 27th of August, this is a motion which was filed at a rather late date and was not translated into one of the two languages of the Tribunal -- this is just as a parenthesis that I've opened here, but having heard the comments of both parties and the comments included within the brief and the responses to the brief, we have decided to reject the brief, and we order that the trial be continued, for the three following reasons. The Judges, first of all, have in their mind the rights of the accused. The rights of the accused are not only not compromised by this decision, but to the contrary, are safeguarded. The Judges first find, under Rule 73 ter, in the pre-Defence conference, that the Defence has the opportunity at the proper time, in light of what will have taken place during the presentation of evidence by the Prosecution, will have the opportunity to provide the Judges, in closed session, with a complete account of anything that may have happened, anything that may be lacking, lacking because the witnesses may not have been able to be cross-examined properly. But at that point, they can be called back for a hearing with both parties present. The Judges would also like to say that the Defence can call the witnesses back if that should be necessary, even if this might appear difficult. The request can be made, and this is a right of the Defence, that is, to call witnesses and to call them again under the supervision of the Judges. Lastly, the Judges point out, keeping mindful of the rights of the accused, that the Defence can also bring in any other witness who, depending upon the events that occurred on that territory in that region, would allow, after a justification, a supplement to be made to the Defence list. This is the first part of our reasoning. The second group of reasons has to do with the Judges' role in this Tribunal. The Judges receive, from the Rules and from the Statute, rights given to them by the Security Council, and those rights are that they shall ensure an equitable, fair, expeditious trial, but a fair one, and this means with both parties having absolute equal footing. Under this reasoning, the Judges first of all go back to Rule 98, which allows the Judges to call in -- empowers the Chamber to order production of additional evidence. The Trial Chamber may order either party to produce additional evidence. It may, proprio motu, summon witnesses and order their attendance in light of the debates, and if necessary, the Judges will use Rule 98. As guardians of an equitable trial, one finds this marked in 89(D), which, if necessary, allows the Judges to exclude any evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial, of which they are the guardians, guardians of the fair trial. The Judges also go back to 90(D)(i). I could say that "The Trial Chamber shall exercise control over the mode and order of interrogating witnesses and presenting evidence so as to make the interrogation and presentation effective for the ascertainment of the truth"; as I say, for the ascertainment of the truth. And I would like to add that ascertainment of the truth is a notion which exceeds, of course, both the interests, which are well understood, of the Prosecution and the accused. And, lastly, the third group of reasons goes back to the higher interests of justice, of which the Judges are also guardians, and it is in that respect that the Judges must take into account the situation of the witnesses, who very frequently are victims, and this means that they must be heard in the order that was set. And it's for all of these reasons that the Defence brief of Defence counsel for Mr. Jelisic has been rejected, and we order that the trial continue as had been scheduled. Mr. Nice, I give you the floor, not in order to make any comments about a decision which was just taken, but simply to tell us what the conduct of the trial will now be. I suppose it has to do with calling a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. There are a couple of administrative matters that I'd like to deal with first. Number one, the Court gave leave for the case officer, Mr. O'Donnell, to be present in court under 90(E). At present, Paul Basham, who sits behind me at the moment, is the case officer. May I have leave, in place of Mr. O'Donnell, for Mr. Basham to sit in court throughout? It's very helpful to me and I think important that that should happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No observations to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No comments by -- how do you pronounce his name again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Basham, B-A-S-H-A-M.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Basham, who will now join the Prosecutor's bench, and we wish to welcome you to your new post.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second point. We, on the Prosecution side, have been aware for some weeks that there are three weeks of trial sittings planned for this case, starting today. I understand that the Defence may be in a different position, not being aware of the third week. One of us must be wrong. We understand it to be three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As late as Wednesday of last week, I spoke to the Defence Counsel Liaison Unit, and they told me that there was no sitting set for the third week, and we've had no notification of any kind that there is due to be a third week. If there is such a third week, it may cause a number of difficulties certainly to me. We've been operating on the basis that there would just be two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you give some clarification? I thought we were supposed to work until the 20th or the 15th or 16th of September. 18th of September, that's what my colleague Judge Riad has just reminded me of.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, until the 17th, that was the 17th, which is a Friday in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And was this information given in proper time to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Ordinarily, I know that those three weeks had been set around the middle or the end of July, unless I made a mistake, as regards the three weeks of trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Londrovic, were you informed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that that microphone --

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I talked today with Mr. Rohde at quarter to 2.00, that is, about 15 minutes before the trial, and he told me that he knew that this stage of the trial would last two weeks. And Mrs. Monika as well referred to two weeks. We have received no notification in writing. We also do not know if additional witnesses, which we see on the Prosecutor's list, have been approved. I do not know which witnesses are protected, whether protection was sought for some of the witnesses. I do not know if I'm allowed to pronounce their names in public, but some witnesses were not on their previous list and now I see them on this list, and I do not know whether the Chamber has approved the new witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges ask questions in this court, Mr. Londrovic, ordinarily. The Judges are here for three weeks for the Jelisic case. Can you now make preparations for the third week, Mr. Londrovic, Mr. Greaves, assuming there was a mistake on the Registrar's part? I don't really know. Mr. Fourmy is not here today, but it seems to me that we had spoken about those three weeks quite a long time ago. In theory, we will do three weeks of trial now. I can tell you that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, we can only deal with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: [Inaudible] official information is forthcoming, and we haven't had any official information that there is to be a third week. One may talk of something as a possibility, but that possibility does not become a certainty until it is issued as a formal document saying, "This is the schedule. This is the order that we give as to the schedule." Counsel can only operate on the basis of official information, and none of that has been communicated to us. Plainly, the Defence Counsel Liaison Unit is in ignorance of the existence of this third week, because I checked last week, my learned friend Mr. Londrovic checked today. They don't know about it and so we don't know about it. We can only operate on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, how many witnesses do you plan to call during those three weeks?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have, I think, available over 20 witnesses. We are calling them in batches, and we are expecting to be able to move witnesses forward at quite a rate by a technique that I hope to reveal to you in a minute and also by focusing on the central evidence of each witness and only on the central evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you are confirming that the Defence was aware of a decision which I rendered on the 27th of April, 1999, when you only added three witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. I misunderstood your first question. No, as to the additional witnesses. Mr. Londrovic's observations in relation to the weeks of trial included the separate issue of witnesses not on the original list. There are names not on the original list. I was hoping to be able to deal with those in an application tomorrow. In summary, the grounds of the application would be that there being witnesses who have refused, there being the real prospects of getting to the heart of the evidence in the case of all these witnesses more swiftly, and fundamentally that these other witnesses can give short but extremely valuable evidence to the Tribunal, I would be asking, and I think tomorrow, that their names may be added. But I would prefer to deal with the matter tomorrow not least because I hope to discuss the matter more fully with my learned friends, both in relation to witnesses who aren't here and in relation to the parts of the evidence of the proposed additional witnesses that might either be the subject of agreement or, in any event, that might be the subject of agreements to their being called. So that I have available, subject to the addition of those names, over 20 witnesses. I am reasonably confident that we will be moving at a far faster speed in this case than perhaps in any or most other cases and that we will get to the heart of the evidence, and therefore there are available over 20 witnesses, including the odd expert witness, to fill this three-week period. I have a particular observation to make about the expert witness. I might as well deal with it now. I have been concerned that the subject of exhumation, which is subject of expert evidence, would appear not to be the subject of any direct contradiction. I've discussed the matter with Mr. Greaves, and we are always able to discuss matters frankly, but it would appear, and I can't be sure about this, it would appear that on the expert evidence of exhumation, I am, in the terminology of the common-law system, for what that's worth, I am being put to proof. That is to say, I've simply got to put the evidence before you, even though it may not be challenged. I am concerned about that, because the evidence will have to be called from Australia. The witness concerned will have to come all the way around the world, and it seems to me undesirable, in the setting of this type of tribunal, that matters that may not truly be in dispute should only be available at such expense and, indeed, extravagance, so I was going to invite this Tribunal, at some stage this week when the evidence had started to unfold, to consider whether it should enquire of the Defence whether they really had a case to put in relation to the scientist or whether the Prosecution was simply being put to proof, because of course it's always open to the Tribunal to admit evidence in hearsay form. I mention that because I had this in mind for the timetable, and I haven't yet, as it were, summoned the witness from Australia and I've got him on hold until next week when I must tell him whether to come or not. Subject to that problem, which I would rather again put off until a little later this week, I've got witnesses to fill the three-week period with evidence for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that clarification. The schedule had been set. I don't know if there was a mistake in its remission, but you must understand, Mr. Greaves, that this is now the 30th of August and we're talking about the third week of September, which would be from the 13th to the 18th. I believe those are the dates, 13th of September until the 17th of September. So, in principle, you have time to make your preparations, assuming that there was a mistake in the information being transmitted. I see the possibility of saying to you that we decided on the 27th of April that we would add three witnesses. I had rendered a decision with my colleagues to add three witnesses to the Prosecution list, whose names you were given. Therefore, you should, in theory, be prepared for these three weeks. That's all the more important, because these three weeks should close the cycle for the Prosecutor's presentation of his evidence, and that would therefore allow you calmly, because we did not prepare for any hearings after that, to organise. We will have a Status Conference where you can raise any problems you had during this first phase of the trial. So therefore, in theory, we're going to work for three weeks until the 17th of September. As regards the other questions raised by Mr. Nice, we can go back to them tomorrow, but for right now I can say that we will sit for three weeks, that is, until the 17th of September, a Friday. I ask that you prepare for that schedule. You have heard there is witness statements. You'll know what they are going to say. You'll be in a position to cross-examine them, and I suppose that you will be able to figure out a way to use the third week. Otherwise, the trial would be delayed. Once again, I feel that that is inappropriate in respect of the text that I've just recalled in the previous decision. If there are no further comments, perhaps we're going to suspend for a few moments in order to -- we have to think about the interpreters. We would be ready to hear the first witness. Is that going to be a private session or a public session? Let me say this for the public gallery, that we want the public to know what is going on with our work. I think this is going to be testimony given in private session. That means that there will simply be voice distortion. Is that correct, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Court pleases, this witness would like face distortion and a pseudonym. Pseudonyms A to B have been used but C to E were allocated on the last occasion, and if it's not inconvenient, may this witness become Witness F? If you would prefer him to be Witness C in order to remind yourselves of the order of witnesses, I'm sure we can reallocate them, but by an earlier order, other witnesses were given the initials C, D, and E. Can I just explain very briefly, before the Court rises, what tool I am in a position to provide, I hope, to help with this and with other witnesses, if the tool is of use to this Chamber. It has been tried elsewhere with some success. A minute of explanation will help. Witnesses typically make two, sometimes only one, sometimes more statements. It's necessary to summarise, from all those different sources, what the witness will say. The practice within my team here is that that preparation is done in advance of the witness coming, and so a summary of what it is expected that's material to the case that the witness will say can be prepared before his or her arrival. But of course the witness then needs to check that that summary is correct, may add to it, may correct it, may detract from it, and so the final summary of a witness's evidence can only be prepared when the witness is here. Nevertheless, it is possible for typed summaries of what a witness is expected to say to be available both to the Defence and to the Chamber. Indeed, it should have been possible for those summaries to be available today in B/C/S, French, as well as in English, for I had the first drafts translated into those languages in advance and the translation department was hopeful it would be able to meet my requests to bring the final versions before the Chamber today. In the event, the final versions won't be available until tomorrow morning. May I nevertheless hand in three English and one French version marked "First Draft" in green and explain how, if you find these helpful documents, they may assist us. Judge Jorda --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, yes, that's the way to work, and I would have encouraged you to do that. This is what this Trial Chamber wants and to go right to the very heart of the statements and the testimony of the witnesses and to say what he has to say and not to tell us his whole life, because it's a very complex issue, it's very sensitive issues, and it's very difficult for the Judges to interrupt a witness who was an unfortunate victim of these events. I always ask, before the witness comes, that I be given a written summary, and I want that the examination go to the very heart of the evidence that you're trying to show. Ordinarily, our text tells that the cross-examination must come only after the examination in chief. I think this is a subtle rule and we don't always use it, but we will try to apply this as properly as possible, always keeping in mind the rights of the accused. However, ordinarily, with the summary and properly-targeted questions targeting the essential questions for which the witness came to The Hague to testify about, and with the cross-examination and the examination in chief, we should be able to go quickly and equitably, which would allow the Prosecution and the Defence to present their points of view. Do you have any other clarifications you would like to provide, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only this, that if you take the version not presently before you for Witness F, the name should be struck through. If you take that version before you, bearing in mind that the French may be marginally different because it's the first draft from the English, the final version of the French and B/C/S available tomorrow, what it will be possible for us to achieve, I think, with the cooperation of Mr. Greaves and Mr. Londrovic, which I know will be forthcoming, is to say, for example, "Well, paragraphs 1 to 5 are non-contentious," if that be the case, and then I can simply summarise those to the witness, the witness says, "Yes, that's true," and we go to page 2. That's what I intend to do, if that's acceptable to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My colleagues agree with me. Any comments or objections, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: None as to that procedure, but there are two matters that I wanted to raise of an administrative nature before Your Honours rise, please. The first is this, that my learned friend Mr. Londrovic and I don't have a common language. We do have an interpreter. I've asked my learned friend for the Prosecution if he has any objection and he has not, but would Your Honours permit my interpreter to sit with us at counsels' bench? Would you think that was a proper thing to do, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there's no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But I just, and I don't want to harp on it at any length, deal with the question of schedules. Your Honour, it's not so much a matter of preparing for witnesses. If counsel aren't informed what the schedule is, we tend to make other arrangements with our life, both professionally and privately, that now have to be unpicked if that information is not forthcoming. It is, as I said much earlier this year, very important that good advance notice be given to counsel. This is not a court where we arrive or practice in the same town and can simply arrive at the drop of a hat. Some of us live elsewhere in the world, and it causes considerable inconvenience if we have to, at very short notice, rearrange other matters. Can I make that clear and ask that if there are to be further schedulings, they be given in good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the future, of course, assuming that there was an error. I want to wait for Mr. Fourmy in order to be sure whether or not there was an error on the part of the Tribunal's administration. I would be very sorry if there were, but that doesn't change the Judges' resolve to have the three weeks of trial, unless something unexpected happens that we cannot control. If there are no further comments, I believe we can now adjourn for 15 minutes. Yes, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise, but you said a while ago that you had allowed the Prosecutor to add three witnesses to the list, and this is not in dispute. However, I see some other names on their list, and I do not know that the Chamber has decided anything on them. I repeat, I do not want to read out these names because I do not know if they are protected, but there is 16, 17, 18, 19, and 20. It is five new witnesses, and this is the first time we've absolutely heard about them or seen their names. We do not know when they were added to the list, and we do not know yet if you will approve it. We do not know if, under Rule 73, the Prosecution was allowed to do it, but I do not really know those new witnesses that Mr. Nice refers to. When I count them, I see 12 or 13 witnesses, without the five expert witnesses, that is, and yet my learned friend is referring to about 20 witnesses. Now, if some new witnesses are going to be added, of course it is up to the Chamber to do so, but I'm afraid the Defence is really placed in an inequitable position in this matter. I did not know about the three weeks of hearing or else I wouldn't have bought a return ticket to return to Herzegovina on September 13th, and I do have this ticket. So it is quite evident I knew nothing about those three weeks. As for the statements which are not in dispute, I'm afraid this might arise as a problem, because we do not know what our learned friends have prepared as indisputable, but we should indeed like to receive those lists both in English and in our language and then discuss it with them to see whether these statements are in dispute or not in dispute. We shall be seeing them only tomorrow, but we shall need, I think, a meeting to discuss them and see whether they are disputable or not, and I'm not sure whether we can agree with this manner of work. I'm not sure we can do that. If my learned friend from the Prosecution believes that he will now introduce here the practice used in Mr. Kordic's case, if that is the system of work that is proposed by the Prosecution, then I believe this was rejected by the Chamber, if I am correct, that is, if that is the method you are proposing. Now we really do not know which sequence will be followed, which witnesses are relevant, which are not, which were approved by the Chamber, which were not. We simply do not know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, would you like to make any further comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are two issues again. Certainly so far as the summaries are concerned, I can make available, I think, to Mr. Londrovic a first draft of the summary in the same way as I made a French version available to the Court, and I hope that will help him for this afternoon. As I've already indicated as to additional witnesses, I would prefer to deal with that matter tomorrow, having discussed the matter with my friends, but I recall having a fairly extensive discussion with Mr. Greaves towards the end of the last term, as it were, and ended up by my sending him a letter. Neither of us has the letter, I think, in court today. I certainly raised with him then that there would be an application to deal with additional witnesses at the beginning of the trial. So I would hope that we can satisfy Mr. Londrovic's concern about a summary by providing him with a first draft of the B/C/S when the Court adjourns and deal with additional witnesses tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As much as possible, I would like for you to come to an agreement. Let me remind you that the witness list was set up during the Pre-trial Conference pursuant to Rule 73 bis. It's always difficult to add witnesses. We did that on the 27th of April, Mr. Nice, at your request, through a decision that the Judges rendered, but of which the Defence could have been informed well in advance. Each time a witness is called in, then the order of the scheduling is disrupted, and you know that the Judges in this Trial Chamber want the trials to come to a proper end. If, once the trial begins, new things are added, new witnesses, new evidence, or even investigations are continued, I cannot see how one can ensure that the trial is conducted properly, and I think, Mr. Nice, you have to try to counterbalance things here in order to make things easier. Perhaps the problem of additional witnesses will be taken up tomorrow, but for the time being, what I would wish is for this trial to begin, and I would like the interpreters to be able to take a break. We'll take a 15-minute pause, and we'll start at 20 after 4. Nothing prevents either of you coming to an agreement on the additional witnesses. I'm speaking of Mr. Nice and Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can resume the hearing now. Please have the accused brought in. We will now have the accused brought in. Let me say this for the gallery. We will raise the curtains. They were simply lowered so that when the witness comes in he not be identified, that is, that nobody in the gallery be able to see who it is. All right, Mr. Prosecutor, we're not going to go back to the summary, as I did in other trials, because you have given us in French, for which I'm very appreciative, and this will allow us to speed up the witness testimony. This is Witness F; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, Mr. Registrar, would you have the witness brought in to the courtroom, please. That is, Witness F.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Let me mention that we can number the summaries that were given to you. There would be Exhibit 8, Prosecution Exhibit 8. Exhibit 7 was identification of the witness's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you putting a reference number both on the English and French versions?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. I thought that there was a French and English version but also one in B/C/S, in which case the -- well, everything will depend on the original. I think that the B/C/S would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. You don't have to explain what you're going to do; just be sure that it's done. All right. This is Exhibit 8, the summary. The witness is going to come into the courtroom now. Can he be brought in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, please do not sit down. Mr. Usher, he should not -- would you prefer that he sit down? He's going to take an oath seated, then?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, because there are some technical limitations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Do you hear me, Witness F? Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have come to The Hague; perhaps this is the first time. We thank you for it. You're going to take an oath first, and then you're going to identify your name on a piece of paper which is being given to you by the usher, but first I'm going to ask you to take an oath, and under exceptional circumstances, we're going to allow you to remain seated so that your face not be seen. Give the witness the formula. Witness F, you can read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You are now going to identify your name but not say it. Simply check to see that that is, in fact, who you are. Please show him the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. You are being covered by protective measures that you asked for and the Prosecutor asked for on your behalf. You are perfectly protected, at least within the Tribunal, and you can speak now, answering the questions that the Prosecutor is going to ask you, and then you're going to answer the Defence's questions, and lastly you will answer the Judges' questions, if the Judges need to ask you any. Speak without hatred, without fear. Try to relax. You are before a tribunal, before judges. Try to relax and feel comfortable and have no fear. This is all that I can tell you now. If you have any problems, any physical, emotional, or any other type of problems, do not hesitate to say that. If you need to drink something, if you need to take a break, let us know. In any case, try to remain relaxed. And now I believe we can begin, Mr. Registrar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Prosecutor, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness F, in April 1992, did you live in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The bridges were blown up on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Having been advised to leave town, did you move to a friend's apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but this took place later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What day --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What day did you move to the friend's apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The accurate answer is that the war started on the 1st of May. That night I spent in my private home, but there was no protection from the shelling there, so on the next morning, the 2nd of May, we took an opportunity to move over to the apartment of my friend and neighbour who had --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll stop you there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- who was in the basement of the building. So it was safer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there and move on so that we can focus your evidence. Were you and many other people evacuated by Serb military personnel some days later? Just "Yes" or "No."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give the date for that evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the evacuation peaceful or by force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you separated into Serbs and non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were the non-Serbs taken to Brcko barracks, where the males over 18 and under 60 were separated from the other males?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The following morning you were going to one location. Were you in fact put on buses and taken to the Luka warehouse on the river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What number of people, very approximately, were evacuated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between one and two thousand. It is hard for me to tell exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment. Do you mean to Luka, or to the Brcko barracks?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To the Brcko barracks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between one and two thousand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And to Luka itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my estimate, between six and seven hundred men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the barracks, did you learn of or did you see something of a man from the village of Janja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the barracks, but at Luka, because that's where they were calling out the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened to that man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we entered Luka, we had to turn in our personal documents, and then the Serbian soldiers checked the documents. When they saw that this gentleman was from Janja, they called him out and they 130 started beating him. This started in the hangar in Luka first, and then they took him out from the hangar where the rest of us were all put.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see that man again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After he was taken out, we couldn't see, but we heard terrible screams, and this man never came back to this room where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shortly after, did two men enter the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Wearing what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of them was wearing a uniform of the former police force, that was the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and he had a light blue shirt and darker blue pants. He had an automatic pistol with a silencer in his hand, and at his belt he also had a police baton. It was a very large one; I had not seen that length of baton before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did a man say anything? If so, what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this man asked us, "Do you know me?" We responded more or less in unison that we did not, because we didn't; he was not from Brcko. And then he said, "If you don't know me, you will get to know me very well. I am the Serbian Adolf."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he say anything else at that stage about who he was, what he was doing, his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said, "Only about five to ten of all of you who are here will be lucky enough to leave here alive."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he say anything about who was controlling your futures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said something to the effect that our destiny, our fate, was in his hands, and it was going to be in his hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he say anything to his companion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he then said to his companion, "We could start with our work," and then he sent him to bring in a box, an empty box. When this companion came back with the box, he told us, "Anything valuable that you have, gold, money, and such, put in this box, and if anything should be found on any one of you after this, he will be dealt with in short order." And by that he meant he would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did another uniformed person enter the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, right around that time, when they started taking off their valuables and pulling out the money, a uniformed soldier came into this room. We recognised the insignia. He was a member of the so-called military police of the JNA. They had white belts around their waist and across their chest. Shall I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When he walked in, as I said, nobody knew this man who introduced himself as Adolf the Serbian, and then he said, "What are you doing here?" They were starting to loot. He said, "We came from Bijeljina, and while we're here, nobody is to touch them." Then they had a conflict. The man who introduced himself as a Serbian Adolf said, "You don't know me. I only need to make a phone call and then you will learn who I am, and you will see what will happen." After that, the Serbian Adolf left the hangar where we were all staying, and he was very angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In his absence, how were you treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout this time, as people were coming in, everybody was trying -- in fact, I was among the first who came, I was on the first bus. Everybody was trying to go to the back of the hangar because they felt safer there, but everybody who came in had to leave everything of their personal effects, such as documents and if they had any bags, they had to leave them at the door. All this time, the soldiers were perusing these documents, and so they found a personal identity card of this man who they saw was from Janja, and this is why they called him out. I think that the reason for it, as we learned later, was that Janja was a Muslim village near Bijeljina which was the only village which had some weapons and refused to turn it in, and these Serbs, Serbo Chetniks, these paramilitary troops, were very angry at people from this area, and so this is why this young man was called out and taken out, and then he never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it possible for some of you to be released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to clarify things, I would like to point out one thing which I think is very important. The members of the so-called military police of the former JNA were somehow giving us more sense of security. We knew these guys. They were our neighbours from the area where I live, from my neighbourhood, and they treated us correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those of you known to Serbs, were you able or were you at least in a position to have a chance of being released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After a while, they came by themselves and they told us. I personally have the impression that they were looking for a way to help us out in this situation because we knew each other so well, we had grown up together, we were friends, and it is possible that this was a reason why they later came back, and they told us that some will be released and that a Serb will guarantee with his life, but if later it turned out that some of them were members of the SDA or had anything to do with that party, that this Serb was the first who will pay the price by losing his life, and then this person himself would do so. In the meantime, all the documents -- that is, outside we could hear some motor vehicles arriving outside, and at one point the soldiers came in and took all the documents which had been gathered inside. And then in order for us to be released, this man would come in, and they would check and see who they could guarantee for. Then they would leave and then come back with, I don't know, five to ten documents, and these documents were personal identity cards, student cards or passports, and bring them. These documents meant that a person could walk out with it to a table in front of the hangar and get a release document, and with this document they could leave Luka once the transportation was secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you fortunate enough to be called out and to be given a pass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was lucky enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By whom was the pass signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to point out that moment. I think it's very important. I would like to clarify it. When we gave those passes, these release documents, it was a piece of paper 10 by 20 centimetres and it bore a stamp which was unknown to me until then. It said "Serbian Autonomous Region of Semberija and Majevica." That was in the upper corner, and then it would state that such and such person was being released, and then it would state their date of birth and the registration number of his identity card, and then it was signed by Djorde Ristanic, the self-appointed president of the Brcko municipality assembly. I think that this document is very telling in many ways. First of all, the very stamp which did not exist before, and then it was the highest organ of the civilian authority which was on the signature. All this means that there had been preparations, that all this was not haphazard, that there was coordination between the military authorities and paramilitary authorities and civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By whom --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By whom was your pass signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The pass was signed by Djorde Ristanic. After the Serbs took over control of most of the city after the war broke out, he became the self-appointed head of the Brcko municipality, which was the highest local civilian authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look, please, at an aerial photograph which will be placed on the ELMO, although the usher will show you that you must sit in your seat and point to things with a pointer to help us, and this will become Exhibit number, I think, 7 or 8.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I forgot the other two. Thank you so much. If he could have the pointer, please, so he could stay in his seat. Don't move. Otherwise, your face may be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But if you stay in your seat, can you point out, please, the hangar to which you were first taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the first one here [indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where were you made to stand when you got your pass and were standing outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was -- there is an overhang here [indicating] and so this is where a table was put, and a soldier was filling out the passes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you look at this photograph, please, which will become Exhibit 10? Thank you. Does that show the same area, but now at ground level, with the hangars on the left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were standing under the overhang or you made reference to the overhang. Can you point to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was the door here [indicating]. There are sliding doors. They were open, and we were here [indicating] in this front part of the hangar, the first third of it, so we could see very little outside, as we were inside. They were filling out these passes, and the table had been set right here by the door [indicating], and so people --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to interrupt you. When you got your pass, did you wait outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, around here, right close to the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of me was the table, and behind it was this man who was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was happening in the building or office opposite to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we were here [indicating], from here we could hear and see even -- we could hear a lot of noises. It was as if some furniture was being slammed down, and some kind of loud screams, human screams.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Coming from where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Across the entrance to the hangar [indicating], this was the administration building and the cashier of the Luka company, and this is where these screams were coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you, in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around here [indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] -- see several men leave the office opposite at intervals of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I was in this place, I was practically outside, I could see what was going on outside. There was a door there [indicating], and first a man was brought out, escorted by this man who introduced himself as the Serbian Adolf. I did not know his name at that time because he never told us the real name. He only introduced himself as the Serbian Adolf. Again I would like to point out it is clear that we were all very scared because we were facing death and everything was pointing to that, and I would also like to point out that this place, in World War II, this is a location where civilians were murdered during World War II, so it was something that spooked us almost, because of those memories.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did the man called Adolf do to that first man you saw coming out of the office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came out here [indicating]. It was almost directly across from the hangar door. First this man came out. In fact, Adolf was pushing him, was actually nudging him with the automatic pistol, and so he was sort of directing him in which direction he was going to go and they were going down there [indicating], and he was taking him and pointing where he was going to go. Then they turned the corner of the building. You can't see it very well. We couldn't see what was going on behind there, but a couple of seconds later we heard two muffled shots, and then Goran returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The man who was being pushed and who didn't return, did he say anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd say first that he looked awful. He was in such a bad condition that he was barely recognisable. He was covered in blood, dirty, had very many scars on his face, or rather there was blood on his hair, his hands, there were lacerations on his arms, and he was moving in a very unnatural manner, so he must have been very badly injured or something must have been done to him. Goran was pushing him with the pistol and indicating the direction in which he should move, and the man was swearing on the life of his children that he was not a member of the green beret and was imploring Goran, that is, the Serb Adolf, not to kill him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where did the Serb Adolf go when he returned from behind that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he returned from behind that building, he went to this man where they were writing, to this table, where they were writing at this table, so that is rather inside Luka, inside. He was about five or six metres from the table where there was a group of Serb soldiers. They were talking. I don't know what about. But Goran, after he had done that, he approached that group and commented something, and they laughed. I don't know what they were talking about, but I know they were really laughing heartily. It looked like a party. They seemed very amused. I can't explain that, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about the second man that you saw to leave the office. First, how long after the first man did the second man leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the first man left, one heard the same thing all over again, that is, something hitting against pieces of furniture or something and screams. Then, if one can judge it, it must have been some 10 or 15 minutes later when the second man was taken out. They simply pushed him through the door and then Goran approached, and once again the same thing happened. He placed himself behind the victim, then nudged him with the pistol, and then moved or went behind so that you could not see him, and then again one could hear two muffled shots. Then Goran would come back again and reach that group of soldiers who were there, and then they would chat again for a while and laugh as if nothing had happened, as if nothing was happening.
