I remember that he asked us then -- or rather he asked, "What are you doing outside," meaning us who were waiting for those passes, and the guy who was writing the passes told him, "Well, these are men who will be released because a Serb is guaranteeing for them," and then he laughed, turned in our direction and said, "Oh, you are those five per cent of the lucky ones who will survive, and in future when you meet me in the town, you'll treat me to a drink." We said nothing. We just stood there with our heads down. We dared not look at him because that look might draw his attention, and realising what kind of a man he was, of course we were afraid to look at him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The third person to leave the office block, how long later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, but it could have been 10, 15, 20 minutes later. I think the intervals were more or less the same. That is, meanwhile you hear screams, and then the door opens again and the third person comes out and he looks the same, and it almost defies description. Very many lacerations, scratches around the eyes, head, blood on the hair, unnatural posture as if some bones had been broken, and in such a state that they were barely able to move one foot at a time. Again with the pistol in his back, he was directed to move in the same direction, and when they would get out of our sight, then one would hear again those two shots, and Goran would be back alone and would join again that group of soldiers standing outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The fourth detainee to leave the office, tell us about him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fourth victim or, rather, the fourth person, as far as I could see, he looked even worse. That is, he practically could not walk by himself. One of his arms was hanging as if something had been broken and he could not control it. When he came out, Goran pushed him with a pistol and the man simply could not stand on his feet. He did not fall his full length, but he went down on his knees, and Goran was behind him, that is, the Serb Adolf, he was some two or three metres behind him, so he came to him and got him under the armpits to help him stand up so that he could walk again. He had barely done that, he gave a shiver as if when somebody is disgusted by something, and he said something to the effect that, "I must be crazy. I'm helping a balija to stand up and I've got my hands soiled." That man whom he had helped to stand up, he was moving very, very slowly in the same direction as the previous victims. Then he came up very close with his automatic pistol with a silencer, and from very close quarters, at close range, some 20 or 30 centimetres, fired at the back of his head. It is a terrible impact. It's as if you're throwing a man from a height so that he fell. Then he came up to him, straddled the victim and was somewhere at the level of the victim's knees, and then standing above him, he shot him in the back, somewhere in the region of the heart. Then he moved around and showed the two persons who had been issued the passes and were waiting to be released and told them to take the victim behind the corner. So they got the victim under the armpits and drew him around the corner, presumably to where all the other victims -- Goran's victims were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This man who had shot and killed the other man, what did he then do or say and to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among this group of soldiers who were standing there, I think I forgot to say that, before Goran killed this fourth one in front of us, this guy came to the table and called us names: "Balija cowards, why don't you fight? You should fight. You see me; my father is an Albanian, my mother is a Croat, and I am fighting for the Serb army." I think he said something like that, and I also think, but I am not quite sure, that he said his name was Branko. And he showed that he had a very thin leather kind of a choker around his neck. On this leather ribbon there was a bullet, and he said, "I will fight for Yugoslavia until my last breath, and this is the bullet for me if I fail." Of course, we did not comment; we just kept silent because we were afraid that it might be dangerous and that we might provoke them. So when the -- to go back to your question, Goran again approached that group, and at that moment, that Branko -- I'm not quite sure if that was his name, but I just think so, but I saw him approach Branko and tell him, "This is the 68th."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to interrupt you for a moment, Witness F. Witness F, except when you have to indicate something on the ELMO, when you answer, please try to face the Judges. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So he said, "This is the 68th." Please carry on with what was said from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Branko asked, "68th? 68th what?" He was asking the question; he didn't understand what this 68 meant. And Goran said, "Well, the 68th balija. There are 68 balijas less," and said something like, "Oh, Lord, how many more will I have to kill before this is all over?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Anything else said by Branko or the other man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then Branko said -- that is, the person that I think is called Branko -- he told Goran then that if he wanted to take a rest, he was quite ready to take his place, that is, he could go on with his job. And Goran said, "No, no." I mean, this is a job which he doesn't find difficult, and also said that when he felt like having a drink, he would count on him. If the Court will permit me, I should like to add that it's very difficult to describe the conduct of that man, and that Branko too. They somehow behaved as if this was a film rather than real life. They were laughing, they simply laughed at those moments, and it's really beyond comprehension. Goran's eyes, there was something in them which I can't really explain. They looked as if he wasn't quite normal. In his look there was something -- there was something so -- so powerful and so cruel, I mean, his eyes were not laughing, only his mouth was laughing. It is very difficult to explain it. I used to see that kind of thing in films, and that is how I would explain it. I mean, he would laugh, but it would be only his mouth. His eyes were not laughing. It was as if in a man who was not quite normal, that is, the only way how I can explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So we turn to the fifth detainee you saw. How long after the fourth was it that the fifth came out of the office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was -- again, these intervals were all about the same; ten or fifteen minutes, twenty, perhaps. It is difficult to be quite accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened to the fifth detainee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not to repeat myself, it's the same thing. The victim came out through this door [indicating]. Again, Goran came somewhere around here [indicating], midway between where he came out and the place you could no longer see them behind the corner. And that victim here [indicating], perhaps a little bit further down, he nudged with his automatic pistol, thus setting the direction. I want to repeat, again, the victim was again in a very similar condition, barely being able to walk, covered in blood, breathing heavily, all deformed, very unnatural walk. And then, whether he simply didn't feel like walking on foot or whether it was a method of intimidation for us, but then the same thing happened all over again. That is, he put the -- from some 20 or 30 centimetres, that is, at a very close range, he fired at the neck of the victim. The victim fell, face to the ground, and then he came close up to the victim and fired in the back, somewhere in the region of the heart, and would again point to persons amongst us waiting for the release, indicating that we were to take the victim round the corner. Of course, they had to do that. After some ten or fifteen seconds, those guys came back, and meanwhile -- so it was already after 8.00 in the evening. It was getting dark, and naturally we were even more scared than before, because we had been told that the curfew was as of 21.00, and after that, nobody was allowed to move about, and our localities were rather far away from Luka, from that port. We knew that we needed at least two hours to get home on foot, and we were telling those lads who were all the time around here -- I mean those lads from the military police -- "What about the transportation?" Because we were afraid that if --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Taking it short, were you eventually escorted out that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The promised bus never arrived, but then they let us walk out, except that the military police kept walking around us, driving around us in a car, and we had to go through countless checkpoints of the Serb army and Chetniks so that we would be effectively prevented from getting home within the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Back to Luka: After that fifth man had been shot by Adolf, what, if anything, did he do? What happened, if anything, to his gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the fifth victim, they took a guy called Danijel for interrogation. He was a resident of Kolobara. And he was beaten. I guess that a door must have been left open so that we could hear better. He was subjected to a severe beating. They had found an automatic pistol on him, and they were asking him where did he get it from, and asked him to admit that he was a Green Beret, or why had he bought that pistol? And he was screaming and repeating, saying that he had never intended using it against the Serb forces, that he had only got it in order to protect his family, his wife and his children. And at that moment we were released, so that I do not know. I heard that he had been killed, but at that moment we left Luka, so I cannot really say anything specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My question, though, was: What did Adolf do after killing the fifth man, and what, if anything, did he do with his gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That person who introduced himself as the Serb Adolf turned over his automatic gun with a muffler to a person whom I remember going by the name Branko, and told him, "There. Now is your chance to make a notch on the butt, because after you kill your balijas, your Muslim persons, then you should know the number." And he said that he was going to have a drink and this Branko would relieve him. And at that moment we were released, so that I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Convert what you've described into a sketch that I think you drew, and we can deal with this exhibit very swiftly. Was this drawn by you or by someone at your direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I drew that with my own hand when I made the statement to the United Nations authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see the hangar, the lane or roadway, and we can see the offices above it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the hangar [indicating]; this is the entrance door [indicating]; and across is the Port Authority building, the administrative building, that is. And this is the corner [indicating] around which Adolf would disappear with his victims and come back. And this is roughly where they took out the victims [indicating]. So he would take this direction, this lane [indicating], and then turn the corner, and we wouldn't see him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see between the office and the hangar -- it's not very clear on our screens, but I think you've written the numbers 4 and 5; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That represents what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the place where, in front of our eyes, Goran killed victims number 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We can also see, just before turning from this exhibit, little blocks at the top of the exhibit marked houses. Can you remember if those were visible from the roadway where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up to a point. That is, these houses were on a slight elevation, on a slope, so that I think -- I believe that we could see some of those houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness please see an exhibit already produced, Exhibit 3. I have spare copies if anybody is short of one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two things, and only two things. How does the gun you can see there compare with the gun you've spoken of? And if you look at the right-hand side of the man there, how does the baton we can see hanging there compare with the baton you've described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the so-called Scorpio, that is, an automatic gun. I'm very familiar with it because when I served in the Yugoslav People's Army, I had it as my personal weapon. It is an automatic pistol, and it can fire individually. It has a regulating mechanism and it has a butt. Here it is [indicating]. It is pulled out, and in front, you have the muffler mounted. You can see it very well. The baton is a baton, that is, a stick. It looked just like this one, except that you can't see here on this photograph, it was much longer. I don't remember ever seeing a policeman who was carrying such a long baton.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. On your walk or march away from Luka through the various checkpoints, did you hear something of the identification of one of the people who had been killed or who was known to be killed? Paragraph 31 in the summary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as we walked in the column -- when leaving Luka, that is -- I heard as we were walking, from people who carried the killed victim, that -- they looked very bad. They looked very bad. They were shaking with fear. They said that there were about 20 people piled up, and that they saw a huge black stain near that group, as if something had been washed with oil or petrol, and that they felt the stench of a burned human body. They were really scared stiff. They were shaking as they were talking. And one of them -- I don't know his name; I can't recall it -- he said -- I mean, as they were telling us this story, they mentioned a couple of names. I remember one, and that is Jasmin Cumurovic,

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted). And another name that they mentioned, I can't remember it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two more exhibits, each of them a list of names. I can certainly deal with one this afternoon, but I wasn't alert to the need to produce the other one; it might be more convenient to deal with it tomorrow morning, if that's acceptable to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to work until 6.00. Let me remind you of that. Don't we go until 6.00, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we continue until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecutor's Exhibit 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness F, were you asked this morning to look at a list of names in alphabetical order that looked something like but wasn't exactly the same as the list before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can show the original version -- in fact, I think I have already shown the version to Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you look through that list to see whether there were any names on the list who were known to you or whose fate was known to you? Can I therefore take you to certain names and invite you to tell us what you know, if anything, of what happened to these people, and also how you got to know of it, if you can now remember. On that first sheet -- and as the Court will appreciate, another witness or witnesses will be producing the original version of this list, which has been simply typed up to make it more legible -- but four up from the bottom, Stipo Glavosevic: What can you tell us about that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew this gentleman very well because we

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted). He was a lawyer. And I also heard from friends and acquaintances that he was killed at Luka; not only was he killed, but he was first tortured, that he was beaten very badly, and that his ears were eventually cut off, that he had covered his ears with his hands when the blood started coming out of them, and that he apparently asked these Serbian killers to kill him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that one of them did, eventually. I was told this by another co-worker. He said that the Serbian soldier told him to kiss his boot and then he would kill him. Then he did kiss his boot and was killed by this soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The following name on the list, Mehmed Glinac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What can you tell us, if anything, about that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell that (redacted) (redacted), and that I saw him at Luka when I was there, that he had been brought there, and then I do not know anything about him. I have not heard anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you could turn to the second sheet of this list, please. There are, five or six lines up from the bottom, there are two names, Kartal, and one name, Kevric. Are those names known to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about the first two names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kasim and Rasim Kartal were two brothers whom I knew rather well because my parents and their parents were very good friends. And I can also say that I don't know anything about their fate. I believe that they are still considered as missing, so nothing is known.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But they were people known to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next name, Sead Kevric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also knew Mr. Kevric, but -- I got to know him very well because he lived in my neighbourhood, but I cannot tell you anything about his fate. I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, I think, over two sheets to page number 4: Does the name "Terzic" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are several persons named Terzic. They were all brothers. I saw them at Luka. I personally do not know what happened to them, but I heard from many people that they were all killed. A lot was said about that because it was a family tragedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the purposes of ease of our recollection, that's the longer list, the 100-plus list. The next list, which I now produce, is a shorter list, I think 39, again --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hesitate to rise and interrupt my learned friend. I notice from the list -- can I draw your attention to page 4 -- that there are two sets of names which are very similar. I want it clarified which set of names he is talking about, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Of course. Would you just return to the previous exhibit, and if you would like to place sheet 4 of the previous exhibit on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you were speaking of the brothers whose fate was well known, you said, can you point out which ones you were speaking of? That's T-E-R-Z-I-C.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. These are the Terzic brothers, Ekrem, Enes, and Muhamed. These are the persons I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Mr. Greaves, because we must then turn to the next one, Tursic. Do you know something of either of those two names, Aldin or Almir, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only say that the Tursic brothers lived very close to where I did, (redacted). I saw both of them at Luka, and never again. I don't know what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, to your knowledge, have you seen any of the names on this list which you were first invited to look at this morning, have you seen any of the names on this list since Luka, since your time in Luka? My mistake. I think my microphone may have been off. Have you seen any of the names on this list since your time in Luka, Witness F?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among the persons who we mentioned, not one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 13, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you were asked to look at this list of names shortly and only this afternoon; is that correct? But are some of the names familiar to you? And I think we start at Number 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and if you would like just to point it out on the list so that we can be quite sure we're looking at the right name. Number 2 on the list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's Number 2, Ahmed Hodzic, also known as Papa. I knew him well from before, and he lived in the Kolobara neighbourhood. He was a member of the resistance against the Serbo-Chetniks. He defended his neighbourhood, and I know that he too was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Numbers 6 and 7, were their names known to you? Do you know what, if anything, happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These are -- I don't know. I know these persons, but I don't know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 8, was that person known to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well, yes, I know him very well. He was also brought to Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as you know, what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He too was killed. I was told this later by some friends of mine who also knew him quite well. Apparently, he was accused of being an activist of the party, and as far as I know, he was not. He, like all of us, he was just somebody from the town and wasn't particularly active. This is why -- this explains -- the fact that about 10.000 Muslims stayed home says clearly that they did not expect this, that they were very naive, and they paid with their lives for that. Those are the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sheet 2, number 16.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Sakib Becirevic, also known as Kibe, he worked as a butcher for the same company and was killed. The word is that a Ranko Cesic, the other person who is wanted by this Tribunal, was the one who killed him. This is what is well known there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 19, 20, and 21 you've already referred to on the other list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the three Terzic brothers who were also killed. That is certain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Vasif Sulejmanovic, also well known in the town because he worked at the local Brcko TV station, and he was also killed later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Over the page to number 33?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Himzo Kevric, also well known in Brcko. He was a merchant, very well known, and I also knew him well because I was very close with his sons, and I came in and visited him often. He worked in the Serbian part of -- he lived in the Serbian part of town near Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Osman Vatic, also well-known figure in town. He was an attorney at law. He headed a law office in town. He was well liked. Terrible stories are being told about his fate, not only that he was killed but that along with his wife, he was tortured for a very long time, abused in many ways, and then only in the end killed. Because he was a wealthy man, he was kept alive until he gave them his Mercedes car, his gold, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 39?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 39 is Izudin Brodlic, also a very well-known person in our town. He had a private shoe shop, so that people in Brcko knew him very well. He was also killed in his house, as far as I know. He also lived near the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. You've spoken of the man who you knew because he was introduced or he introduced himself as Adolf, but you've spoken of him using another name. Where did you get the other name from and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After my release from Luka, I went back to my friend's apartment where I had been before I was taken to the prison, that is, to Luka, and this is very dangerous. Very often Serbian soldiers, Chetniks, paramilitaries, would come in, and they behaved in all different kinds of ways. It was very dangerous being a Muslim there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: would take us there in his own car, and this is what happened. 2 (redacted) was there, and only because he knew me so very well and he had some integrity, he took us in and said that we could work there, but we didn't leave the premises because it was very dangerous. Also later other people who worked at (redacted) were released and who were essential for certain types of work, and so it is from them that I later learned that the person who was calling himself the Serbian Adolf was actually called Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That concludes what I want to ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder whether you want me to start this evening or want to hear it all in one go, rather than have it in two disjointed -- one small bit and then a longer bit tomorrow. I'm entirely in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there is still ten minutes, and you can begin. Every minute is precious. You know that. Yes, please proceed. Witness F, Defence counsel for Goran Jelisic are going to ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness F, just help me, please, if you will. If there is a question of mine which you don't understand, please don't be shy. Just stop me straightaway and ask me to explain it again. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would like to ask you first of all, please, when you made a statement to the International Tribunal, I think you were then in the BiH army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Are you still in that employment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never employed by the BiH army. I only defended my people and my country against the occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I perhaps put it badly, but are you still serving in the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because there is no need for it any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, please, this: As far as yourself is concerned, I think you're now about 38. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. I don't want to get into the exact dates, but I think you were born in September 1961.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You would therefore have been 30 at the time of the war in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I ask you this, Witness F: Prior to May 1992, were you personally involved in politics in any way --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: -- or a member of a political party before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you become a member of any political party during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Since the war, have you become a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was never politically active or a member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want now just briefly to ask you some questions about the period immediately before the beginning of fighting in Brcko. You were asked by my learned friend about the events in late April 1992. At that time prior to the blowing of the bridges that was described to you, were you aware that there was about to be fighting in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. One could assume that, I guess, but I didn't know or nobody knew that this would happen. Otherwise, I would not wait for them to do to me what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course. Just this, please, Witness F: You say that you could assume that there was going to be something happening. Was that because you were aware of the political developments taking place in the Brcko area or because of the wider picture of what was happening in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I felt, like any citizen of Bosnia at that time, that the situation was becoming serious and dangerous in a way, but I believe that essentially my answer is very simple. I did not want a war, and I perhaps would -- I perhaps assumed that there would be some minor skirmishes or duels between the extremist factions, but I didn't think that that would actually happen. Otherwise, I wouldn't have stayed at home. And tens of thousands of Bosniaks stayed home, and when people came to their homes, they still did not believe that something like this would happen, things that did happen later. It is a fact that tens of thousands of Bosnian Muslims, together with their families, stayed in the municipal area at the mercy of the Serb Chetnik occupiers, and I think that that is very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness F, I just want to ask you this very briefly about one of the lists that you've been examined about today, and I'll return to it in due course. But the second list that you went through, the one that you looked at this afternoon for the first time, that's a list containing a number of people who were active in either local affairs or political affairs? Would this be right, that those people that you knew on that list, those people were involved in politics; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Frankly, I believe they were not, because were they politically involved and if they knew what was going to go on, I don't think that they would share the fate of all the victims, which they eventually did. So logically speaking, I don't think it makes sense that they were politically involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You've told us that you were conscious of the picture of what was developing in the wider Yugoslavia, and I perhaps asked the question badly, but were you also aware of political developments at a local level in Brcko, you yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think you just reminded me of something quite important which cost many people their lives. The conflict officially started on 1 May between 4.00 and 5.00 in the afternoon. This is when officially the shooting started and the shelling started. In the course of that day and even in the following day, the conflict was broadcast in the media, and it was said that the members of all the political parties, that is, all three parties in Brcko, were reported to have agreed to a division of Brcko. And it is not something that I need to go into, but I believe that that was part of the reason why so many people believed in it and stayed home and eventually became victims of the treachery and genocide. This is what I'm certain of, but I believe that this is a wholly different subject matter, so that -- the local politics, I believe. The point is the Serbian side always had the position of force because they knew that they had the JNA behind them with their military might, because the Serbian population was in minority in the Brcko municipality, only 20 per cent, and it is absurd that they should still call Brcko Serbian when the last census clearly points to the overall structure of the population in Brcko. Despite all of that, I believe that since our population did not want a war, which again is confirmed by this terrible suffering, I believe that our local authorities -- and imagine a town of that size to be divided between the three communities. It is not normal -- it is not possible to retain any kind of normal life there, but I believe that this was a policy of the official government, the government elected in the last election in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in order to prevent the war. I believe and the events show that the Serbs did not need any hostages or needed provocation. Who were we to wage war there? We lived with our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to interrupt you, Witness F. Try to answer concisely. You understand that this is not really a forum here. I understand that you do want to present your ideas and opinions which are respectable and defendable, given all that you have suffered, but I would like us to focus as much as possible on the questions that are asked both by the Prosecution and the Defence. Would you like to add something about the question that Mr. Jelisic's Defence counsel asked or have you more or less finished what you have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can -- I'm finished. I believe that I said everything that I think was essential with regards to Mr. Jelisic, the so-called Adolf. I think I said everything I had to, but I wanted to point out that what I did not see with my own eyes, and these are horrible stories that I heard, I did not mention but I told just what I saw, and as I took a solemn declaration, this is the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and I wish it were otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have not completed with your questions, Witness F, but will resume tomorrow at 10.00 in the morning. I hope that you can rest this evening, and Witness F, you have to come back tomorrow. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 6.04 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 31st day of August, 1999, at 10.00 a.m.
